power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Recent studies show that working memory for meaningful real-world objects can far exceed traditional capacity limits (~4 items) under experimental conditions where items are briefly presented.
In everyday life, however, information often remains accessible, and observers freely choose how much to remember now and how much to inspect later.
Under such unconstrained conditions, people typically memorize only 1-2 items at a time, far below maximum capacity.
Here, we asked how meaningfulness influences strategic memory use during unconstrained memory-guided behavior.
Using a copying task that allows for reinspection of the display, we compared meaningful real-world objects with meaningless (novel-but-realistic) objects matched on low-level visual features.
Across two experiments, meaningfulness increased memory use, boosting it from ~2.5 items (meaningless objects) to ~3.8 items (meaningful objects) per sampling.
Thus, the advantage of real-world objects extends beyond capacity: it changes how people balance memory use against re-sampling of information in natural behavior.
Working memory, the cognitive system that keeps information in mind to guide behavior, has been classically characterized by a limited capacity (~4 items; Luck & Vogel, 1997).

text.text: Traditionally, working memory studies used simple, abstract stimuli (e.g., colored squares) in single-shot encoding tasks, such as change detection (e.g., Luck & Vogel, 1997) and delayed estimation (e.g., Zhang & Luck, 2008).

text.text: Over the past decade, however, a growing number of studies have investigated working memory in more naturalistic settings.

Two key lines of research have driven this shift: The first breaks away from traditional constraints on stimulus materials, showing that capacity is not fixed but depends on what is remembered (Brady et al., 2016).

text.text: The second breaks away from traditional, single-shot encoding paradigms by allowing participants to remember objects across multiple instances, mirroring the flexible access of everyday information.

When participants can look back at the memory array freely, the number of items that they choose to load into memory (1-2 items) is far below their maximum capacity (Ballard et al., 1995; Draschkow et al., 2021; Sahakian et al., 2023 Sahakian et al., , 2025;; Xu et al., 2025; Qing et al., 2025; Van der Stigchel, 2020).

text.text: Interestingly, these two lines of research, capturing distinct properties of naturalistic memory use, have largely proceeded in parallel, with minimal cross-talk.

This disconnect leaves a core question unanswered: does the well-documented memory advantage for real-world objects in traditional, single-shot encoding tasks shape how we actually use memory during unconstrained memory-guided behavior?

This question can be framed within a cost-benefit account of the memory-sampling trade-off: when sampling is effortless (e.g., requiring only a few saccades), observers remember less at every inspection and instead choose to frequently look back at the tobe-remembered information (Ballard et al., 1995; Sahakian et al., 2023 Sahakian et al., , 2025;; Draschkow et al., 2021; Qing et al., 2025).

text.text: Conversely, when memorization is effortless (e.g., through stimulus repetition), the trade-off shifts toward greater reliance on memory, encoding more items per inspection (Kumle et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026).

text.text: These studies, however, focused on external manipulations (i.e., varying sampling or memorization cost), leaving open the possibility that intrinsic stimulus properties may also influence strategic memory use.

Given that intrinsic stimulus properties can reduce memory cost (e.g., high memorability and low complexity; Ye et al., 2024; Alvarez & Cavanagh, 2004), meaningfulness, a salient property of real-world objects, may similarly lower memory cost and thereby encourage greater reliance on memory.

text.text: Together, these encoding and maintenance benefits should make memory for meaningful objects more robust and less effortful.
We therefore hypothesize that meaningfulness encourages greater reliance on memory during unconstrained behavior.
Specifically, participants should encode more meaningful objects than meaningless ones per inspection and thus revisit the display less often.

To test this hypothesis, we used a copying paradigm (Ballard et al., 1995; Draschkow et al., 2021; Hayhoe et al., 1998; Sahakian et al., 2023) that allows participants to freely choose how much to memorize at every inspection (or how often to look back at the example), directly measuring unconstrained memory use during naturalistic behavior.

text.text: These stimuli match real-world objects on low-level features but lack meaning: they look real but do not exist and do not have associated verbal, semantic labels.

To summarize, we examined how meaningfulness influences memory use (i.e., the trade-off between remembering and sampling) across two distinct levels of spatial organization: between-object arrangements (Experiment 1), in which participants positioned distinct objects to match the example, and within-object arrangements (Experiment 2), in which they reassembled one fragmented object like a jigsaw puzzle.
This dual-level manipulation allowed us to test whether the effect of meaningfulness on memory use is specific to between-object arrangements or also generalizes to withinobject arrangements.
Experiment 1 first examined whether meaningfulness influences strategic memory use in a between-object spatial layout task, where participants placed individual objects in their correct locations.
We contrasted meaningful real-world objects with meaningless novel-but-realistic objects matched to real-world objects on low-level visual features.

We predicted that the lower memory cost of meaningful objects would lead participants to load more objects into memory per inspection and thus look back less often when copying real-world (vs. novel-but-realistic) objects.
The target sample size was set to 20 participants based on prior experience and budget constraints.

text.text: In both conditions, all items in the Model and Resource grids belonged to a single stimulus set (real-world or novel-but-realistic).

Across the 24 trials with real-world objects and 24 trials with novel-but-realistic objects, all 144 real-world and 144 novel-but-realistic stimuli were used only once in the Model grids, with the order randomized between participant.
The 10 distractor items added to the Resources grid on each trial were randomly selected from the same stimulus condition (i.e., real-world or novel-but-realistic) as the target items on that trial.

Distractors were sampled with replacement from the available pool of 256 stimuli in each stimulus condition (400 stimuli minus the 144 used as targets), meaning that distractor images it the Resources grid could appear multiple trials throughout the experiment.
All stimuli were rescaled to fit within the grid cells of the experiment displays.
Procedure.
Before the experiment began, participants received task instructions and completed two practice trials to familiarize themselves with the procedure.
The Model grid, which contained six target items that participants were required to memorize, was covered by a gray square at the start of each trial.
Participants used a computer mouse to reveal the Model grid by moving the cursor over it, allowing them to inspect the target configuration.
Revealing required holding the cursor over the grid for 3 seconds, during which a white progress bar indicated the remaining wait; the target configuration appeared only once this delay had elapsed.
As soon as the cursor moved away, the cover returned and the Model was no longer visible.
Each inspection therefore incurred a 3-second delay, making sampling costly and forcing participants to trade off sampling against reliance on memory.
To reproduce an item, participants dragged an item from the Resource grid and dropped it onto a cell in the Workspace.
When a dragged item hovered over an empty cell, that cell was highlighted in yellow to provide visual feedback.

Upon dropping the item, it was immediately revealed whether the placement was correct: if the item matched both the identity and the location required by the Model grid, it remained fixed in the center of that cell; if the placement was incorrect, the item instantly flew back to its original location in the Resource grid.

Participants could inspect the Model and attempt placements as often as needed until all six target items were correctly positioned in the Workspace, at which point they could click a button to proceed to the next trial.
We use the term "trial" to refer to the entire sequence of placements required to reproduce one entire Model grid configuration.
The main experiment consisted of 48 trials, comprising 24 real-world object trials and 24 novel-but-realistic object trials, presented in random order.
The interleaved design was chosen over a blocked design to prevent the emergence of condition-specific strategies and minimize the impact of learning effects.

To capture the extent to which participants relied on memory versus sampling, we used two main measures: the number of inspections (i.e., views of the Model grid) per trial and the average duration per inspection.

We analyzed these two measures separately because inspection frequency reflects the overall sampling strategy (with fewer inspections indicating greater reliance on memory), whereas inspection duration reflects encoding dynamics.

To assess overall task performance, we measured the total number of placement errors per trial (i.e., item placements that are inconsistent with the Model) and the average trial duration; fewer errors indicate greater effectiveness, and shorter durations indicate greater efficiency.

Data were preprocessed by removing metric-specific outliers (>3 SD from each participant's condition mean) and excluding participants with a median of ≤1 inspection per trial according to pre-established criteria.

text.text: To investigate whether the meaningfulness of real-world objects influences the memory-sampling trade-off (i.e., promotes strategic memory use), we first examined our two measures of sampling behavior: the total number of inspections per trial and the average duration per inspection.

Bayesian paired-samples t-tests revealed very strong evidence that participants made fewer inspections per trial in the real-world object condition compared to the novel-but-realistic object condition (real-world objects: M = 1.98, SD = 0.69; novel-but-realistic objects: M = 2.90, SD = 0.82; 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 1.61 × 10 5 ), see Fig. 3.

text.text: In contrast, when analyzing the duration per inspection, we found only anecdotal, inconclusive evidence for a condition difference (𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 2.78), despite a slight trend indicating longer inspections for real-world objects (real-world objects: M = 7.21, SD = 6.31; novel-but-realistic objects: M = 6.48, SD = 6.56).
These results indicate that meaningfulness of real-world objects leads to a substantially lower frequency of sampling, which was not compensated for by longer inspection times per sampling.
Thus, this demonstrates that participants strategically loaded more items into memory when interacting with meaningful real-world objects than with meaningless novel-but-realistic objects.
To further quantify how many items participants encoded per sampling, we divided the total number of placed items by the number of inspections.

This estimate for real-world objects was ~3.8 items per sampling, which is higher than that for novel-but-realistic objects (~2.5 items per sampling) and than the 1-2 items per sampling typically observed in copying tasks. bars), and participant means (colored dots) for real-world vs. novel-but-realistic conditions across four measures (A-D); gray lines connect individual participant data.
Next, to determine whether this shift in sampling was accompanied by changes in the quality and efficiency of task completion, we assessed overall task performance.

We found very strong evidence that real-world objects yielded fewer placement errors per trial (real-world objects: M = 1.65, SD = 1.63; novel-but-realistic objects: M = 2.37, SD = 1.83; 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 327.09).

Furthermore, there was very strong evidence for shorter overall trial durations in the real-world object condition (real-world objects: M = 42.08, SD = 15.24; novel-but-realistic objects: M = 57.08, SD = 26.02; 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 661.58).

These findings demonstrate that the reduced reliance on visual sampling (mirrored by increased reliance on memory) for real-world objects was accompanied by enhanced general performance (fewer placement errors) and higher efficiency (shorter trial durations).
Real-world memory-guided behavior operates on multiple spatial scales.

Experiment 2 examined whether the meaningfulness of real-world objects also influences strategic memory use in a within-object spatial layout task, where participants reassembled fragments of a single object.
Prior visual experience with an object's typical global structure (e.g., a door) may provide a memory advantage beyond the semantic information carried by isolated fragments (e.g., the door handle).
To test this, we manipulated stimulus configuration (intact vs. scrambled) of both real-world and novelbut-realistic objects.
We predicted that participants would rely less on sampling for real-world (vs. novel-but-realistic) objects, specifically in the intact condition.

A reduction or elimination of this real-world advantage in the scrambled condition would indicate that prior visual experience with global structure contributes independently to strategic memory use, rather than being driven by local semantic features alone.
A new group of 20 participants (mean age = 27.95 years, SD = 4.81; 10 females, 10 males) was recruited via Prolific.

To systematically investigate the mechanisms driving memory-guided behavior, Experiment 2 employed a 2 × 2 × 2 mixed To isolate the contribution of holistic processing, each base image was divided into a 3×3 grid of segments.
In the intact condition, the segments were arranged in their original spatial order, preserving the global structure.
In the scrambled condition, the segments were shuffled, disrupting the global structure.
This manipulation allowed us to test whether any advantage for real-world objects depends on an intact global structure.
Procedure.
Participants were randomly assigned to Stimulus Set A or B, completing a total of 48 trials.

The experiment followed a balanced design, featuring 24 real-world and 24 novel-but-realistic object trials, with half of each stimulus condition consisting of intact images and the other half of scrambled images (i.e., 12 trials for each of four conditions).
Trial order was randomized per participant, in a fully interleaved design.
To verify that participants indeed had prior visual experience with the real-world objects (but not with the novel-but-realistic objects), we included a surprise post-experiment rating task.
This manipulation check was particularly relevant for Experiment 2, in which only 24 stimuli per stimulus condition were used (instead of 144 in Experiment 1).

We therefore included the rating task to confirm that real-world objects were familiar (consistent with prior visual experience), whereas novel-but-realistic objects were unfamiliar to our participant pool.
Participants were presented with all 24 target base images from their assigned stimulus set (in their intact configurations) one by one in a randomized order.
They were instructed to rate the subjective familiarity of each image on a 7-point Likert scale (ranging from1 = completely unfamiliar to7 = highly familiar).

Behavioral performance (i.e., number of inspections, inspection durations, number of errors, and trial durations) was primarily assessed using a 2×2 mixed Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), with object type (real-world vs.
novel-but-realistic) and stimulus configuration (intact vs. scrambled) as within-subject factors.
The critical theoretical focus of this analysis was the two-way interaction between object type and stimulus configuration.
Specifically, we expected performance benefits for real-world over novel-but-realistic objects to be larger for intact than for scrambled objects.
Such an interaction would indicate that the advantage for real-world objects depends on intact global image structure.

In the original 2×2×2 mixed ANOVA, the between-subjects factor Stimulus Set contributed negligibly to all four measures (maximum 𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 1.35) and was dropped from subsequent analyses (see Supplementary Materials S6).

Because scrambling rearranges the exact same physical components of each base image, local low-level visual properties are perfectly matched across intact and scrambled states, so any interaction effect must be attributed to the disruption of global structure rather than to low-level visual confounds.
To verify our stimulus manipulation, we compared subjective familiarity ratings between real-world and novel-but-realistic objects.
Additionally, we conducted exploratory analyses to test whether subjective familiarity was associated with behavioral performance.
The detailed methods, results, and discussion of limitations for these exploratory analyses are reported in Supplementary Materials S7.
We used the same Bayesian approach and evidence classification as in Experiment 1, except that here the data were analyzed using ANOVAs rather than t-tests, due to the factorial design.
Accordingly, we report Inclusion Bayes Factor (𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 ) comparing models with and without the effect of interest.

Akin to the results of Experiment 1, we obtained strong evidence for the main effect of object type (real-world objects: M = 2.54, SD = 0.92; novel-but-realistic objects: M = 3.00, SD = 1.21; 𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 26.24), with realworld objects requiring fewer inspections overall compared to novel-but-realistic objects.

There was also very strong evidence for the main effect of stimulus configuration (intact: M = 1.76, SD = 0.72; scrambled: M = 3.77, SD = 1.54; 𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 4.61× 10 4 ), indicating fewer inspections for intact than scrambled objects.
Moreover, we found moderate evidence for an interaction between object type and stimulus configuration (𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 3.66, see Table 1 for statistical detail).

The analysis revealed strong evidence for a main effect of object type (real-world objects: M = 3.59, SD = 1.56; novel-but-realistic objects: M = 4.85, SD = 2.57; 𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 4.82), indicating that real-world objects elicited shorter inspection durations than novel-but-realistic objects.
Evidence for the main effect of stimulus configuration was inconclusive (intact: M = 4.05, SD = 2.46; scrambled: M = 4.39, SD = 1.99; 𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 0.35).
Moreover, we observed strong evidence for the interaction between object type and stimulus configuration (𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 4.09).

Post-hoc Bayesian comparisons showed that the advantage of real-world objects over novel-but-realistic objects was evident in the intact condition (difference = 2.04, 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 6.13) but was anecdotal in the scrambled condition (difference = 0.34, 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 0.55).
That is, scrambling increased inspection duration for real-world objects (difference = 1.18, 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 9.64) but not for novel-but-realistic objects (difference = -0.53, 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 0.29).

Thus, participants showed an encoding efficiency benefit for real-world objects (shorter inspection durations), but only in the intact condition; this benefit disappeared when the structure was scrambled.
The reduced frequency and duration of sampling observed for real-world objects (compared to novel-but-realistic objects) were not accompanied by a difference in the number of placement errors.
Specifically, analysis of placement errors revealed no reliable differences between conditions.
Bayesian analysis yielded only anecdotal evidence for the main effect of configuration (intact: M = 3.56, SD = 3.06; scrambled: M = 4.59, SD = 3.73; 𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 2.06).
Furthermore, evidence for both the main effect of object type and the two-way interaction was inconclusive (𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 < 1).

text.text: Importantly, this absence of error differences between conditions also rules out the possibility that the observed gains for real-world items in other measures (e.g., fewer inspections) came at the cost of reduced accuracy.

Finally, for total trial durations, there was only anecdotal evidence for a main effect of object type (real-world objects: M = 68.39, SD = 18.91; novel-but-realistic objects: M = 73.41, SD = 19.47; 𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 1.56).

There was very strong evidence for a main effect of stimulus configuration (intact: M = 64.34, SD = 20.76; scrambled: M = 77.39, SD = 18.10; 𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 227.93), so that trials with scrambled objects took substantially longer than trials with intact stimuli.
Importantly, we found moderate evidence for the interaction between object type and stimulus configuration ( 𝑩𝑭 𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒍 = 3.82).

Post-hoc Bayesian comparisons showed that the advantage of real-world objects over novel-but-realistic objects was evident in the intact condition (difference = 10.41, 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 342.65) but was absent in the scrambled condition (difference = 0.50, 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 0.23).
Scrambling increased trial duration more for real-world objects (difference = 17.63, 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 172.56) than for novel-but-realistic objects (difference = 7.71, 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 3.34).

This pattern corroborates that the overall task performance (i.e., trial durations) of real-world objects was better than novel-butrealistic objects only in the intact condition, but not in the scrambled condition.

Together, these findings show that participants (1) performed better and (2) relied more on working memory (and thus less on sampling) when interacting with real-world objects compared to realistic-but-novel objects.
But, these differences between stimulus types were specific to intact images and disappeared when images were scrambled.
To confirm that our real-world objects were indeed related to prior visual experience, we compared post-experiment familiarity ratings between the two stimulus types.

Given the ordinal nature of the 7point Likert scale, mean familiarity scores for real-world and novel-but-realistic objects were computed for each participant and compared using a non-parametric Bayesian Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

Results showed strong evidence that participants perceived the real-world objects as more familiar than the novel-but-realistic objects (real-world objects: M = 6.15, SD = 1.01; novel-but-realistic objects: M = 2.51, SD = 1.90; 𝑩𝑭 𝟏𝟎 = 6.46 × 10 5 ).
This successfully validates our stimulus manipulation, confirming that participants had substantially more prior visual experience with real-world objects than novel-but-realistic objects.

Furthermore, exploratory analyses of the trial-by-trial subjective familiarity ratings showed that higher familiarity was associated with less visual sampling with no costs in accuracy (see Supplementary Materials S7 for full analyses and a discussion of the limitations of these analyses).

Taken together, Experiment 2 replicated the key finding that meaningfulness shifts the memory-sampling trade-off towards greater memory use, extending it from a between-object scenario (Experiment 1) to a within-object scenario.

Dividing the 9 fragments by the number of inspections showed that the familiar intact condition stood out, with participants memorizing on average ~7.5 fragments per sampling, compared with ~6.0 in the novel intact condition and only ~3.3 and ~3.0 in the familiar and novel shuffled conditions, respectively.

These absolute values, however, are not directly comparable to those in Experiment 1 or to the 1-2 items per sampling typically reported in copying tasks, because Experiment 1 indexed whole objects whereas Experiment 2 indexed fragments of a single object, whose encoding may be supported by global configural representations.
In this study, we examined how the meaningfulness of items influences strategic working memory use in natural behavior, where participants are free to decide what to memorize and when.

Across two experiments, we found that participants sampled meaningful real-world objects less frequently (for shorter or comparable durations) than visually matched but meaningless novel-but-realistic objects.
Thus, participants strategically choose to rely more on memory than on external sampling when interacting with meaningful objects.

This strategic shift in memory use was observed both when participants arranged multiple objects in their original spatial locations (Experiment 1) and when they reassembled fragments of a single object (Experiment 2).

Consistent with these results, participants rated the real-world objects as highly familiar and the novel-but-realistic objects as unfamiliar, providing converging evidence that the strategic shift is linked to prior visual experience with meaningful objects.

However, this strategic shift disappeared when the object's global structure was disrupted (Experiment 2), highlighting the importance of (prior experience with) the global image structure of meaningful objects in steering strategic working memory use.

The present findings replicate the memory advantage (e.g., more efficient memory encoding, fewer errors, and shorter task duration) for real-world objects reported in forced-memory paradigms (e.g., Brady et al., 2016 Brady et al., , 2024;; Chung et al., 2023 Chung et al., , 2024;; Morales-Torres & Egner, 2026; Thibeault et al., 2024).

text.text: More importantly, we show that this advantage translates into greater reliance on memory: participants inspected the display less often, without spending more time per inspection.

An alternative was that participants merely exploited the greater encoding efficiency of real-world objects to shorten each inspection without actually increasing the amount of information encoded per inspection-a strategy that would reflect reduced effort rather than enhanced memory load.

Our data show otherwise: in Experiment 1, inspection durations did not differ between meaningful and novel objects; and in Experiment 2 inspection durations even dropped along with the number of inspections, an effect that was not accompanied by an increase in errors.
Thus, the reduced cost associated with memorizing meaningful real-world objects was not used to reduce task effort but to memorize more information per inspection (without compromising accuracy).
Participants inspected meaningful objects fewer times in both experiments, but only in Experiment 2 did they also spend less time on each inspection.
Experiment 2 required participants to encode fragments of a single object, which may be more difficult to distinguish individually.
Retrieving a global template of the meaningful objects from long-term memory may be particularly helpful for recognizing and organizing these fragments, thereby speeding encoding.

Such a template offered less support in Experiment 1, where individual object identities did not predict their locations, and the arbitrary identity-location mappings still had to be learned on each trial, even for meaningful objects.

The scrambling manipulation supports this account: disrupting the global structure abolished nearly all behavioral differences between realworld and novel-but-realistic objects, while preserving all local features.
Thus, neither local semantics nor low-level visual differences can explain the difference in memory use between meaningful and meaningless objects.
Conversely, the advantage in memory use of intact over scrambled images was specific to real-world objects.
Therefore, global structure alone (e.g., Gestalt properties) is not sufficient for driving the observed differences in memory use.
Instead, prior experience with the global image structure of meaningful objects drives the difference in memory use between meaningful and meaningless images.
The vast majority of studies to date studying strategic memory use, in unrestrained tasks (e.g., the copy task) used meaningless stimuli (for an exception, see Koolhaas et al., 2026).

But how might meaningfulness increase the reliance on memory use?

One account is that it lowers the cost of memory by activating structured semantic knowledge (category labels, functional associations, typical structure), expanding representations from a low-dimensional perceptual space to a high-dimensional conceptual space (Chung et al., 2024).

The memory-sampling trade-off, in essence, is a strategic cost-benefit calibration.

Historically, theories of this process have been governed by a constraint-driven framework, wherein observers react to extrinsic task constraints (e.g., physical effort, error penalties, or repetition; Sahakian et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026) and internal capacity bottlenecks (e.g., working memory limits; Böing et al., 2023).

text.text: Critically, this framework treats stimuli as passive placeholders, with strategies dictated solely by environmental costs or memory limits.
The present study broadens this framework by introducing a content-driven dimension: intrinsic stimulus properties alter the memory-sampling trade-off.
Meaningful objects can draw on pre-existing knowledge in long-term memory, making their representations easier to encode and maintain.

This advantage occurs upon first encounter with specific images, showing the effect of preexisting semantic knowledge (e.g., labels, functions, visual familiarity) and contrasting with repetition-based familiarity, which relies on episodic long-term memory built over time (Xu et al., 2026).

text.text: While both long-term memory systems reduce working memory costs, they differ mechanistically: episodic memory retrieves specific learned instances, eliminating active maintenance (Carlisle et al., 2011; Bartsch & Shepherdson, 2022); semantic memory leverages structured category knowledge to immediately expand the dimensionality and stability of working memory representations, reducing interference and encoding demands (Brady et al., 2016; Asp et al., 2021; Chung et al., 2024).

text.text: Thus, observers do not merely react to constraints (in the environment or in their internal capacity); they proactively capitalize on the inherent semantic richness of the visual world to determine how much they rely on external sampling versus memory.
In sum, meaningfulness shapes strategic working memory use by modulating the tradeoff between (internal) memory use and (external) sampling.
The impact of meaningfulness arises even upon the first encounter with specific images, demonstrating an advantage conveyed by long-term memory retrieval, independent of recent exposure.

Breaking away from traditional, 'reductionist' stimuli and forced-response, 'single-shot' paradigms, our findings show that object meaning fundamentally changes how people use memory in unrestrained, naturalistic behavior.
Ultimately, the decision to memorize now (or resample later) is driven not solely by external constraints or individual capacity limits, but also by the intrinsic meaning of the memoranda themselves.
